title: Why you can't just speed up to catch the space station
one_idea: Catching a space station is not about raw speed — it is about timing your orbit so that when you raise or lower your altitude, you meet the station at the same point.
audience_misconception: Most people assume that to reach the ISS faster, you just fly faster — but going faster puts you in a higher orbit, which actually takes longer to circle Earth.

analogy.source_term: The spacecraft goes slower at a lower orbit and completes each lap faster, catching up to the station ahead.
analogy.limitation: Unlike cars on a track, a spacecraft cannot just slow down — it must fire engines to drop to a lower orbit.

claims.claim: The ISS orbits Earth at roughly 7.66 km/s, completing one lap every 90 minutes.
Going faster in space raises your orbit, giving you a longer path around Earth and causing you to fall further behind the station.
Spacecraft catch up to a station ahead by temporarily dropping into a lower orbit, where they travel a shorter path and close the distance.

concepts.name: Orbital speed
concepts.definition: The faster you travel in orbit, the higher your orbit becomes — and the longer your path around Earth.

concepts.name: Orbit phasing
concepts.definition: Temporarily lowering your orbit so you complete laps faster and close the distance to a target ahead in the same orbit.

concepts.name: Space rendezvous
concepts.definition: The process of bringing two spacecraft to the same point in orbit at the same time.

director_notes:
ASSUME: the NASA blog post (source URL https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/spacestation/2026/10/01/dragon-docks-bringing-spacex-crew-13-to-station/) confirms the 8-hour docking timeline; the orbital rendezvous and orbit phasing Wikipedia pages confirm the mechanism.

Format chosen: news_explainer — the Crew-13 docking is a real event (2026-10-01) and the episode's core message is a mechanism reveal, best structured as event hook → misconception → analogy → real mechanism → comparison.

Analogy chosen: racetrack mapping — inner car (slower, lower orbit, more laps per hour) vs outer car (faster, higher orbit, fewer laps per hour); limitation: spacecraft cannot simply slow down, they must fire engines to change orbit.
